title: Inner Dialogues, Monologues and Stone Cold Silence
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explore inner speech (the 'inner monologue' or inner voice), starting with why the term 'inner speech' is preferred and why it is hard to study. They cover researcher typologies such as the VISC questionnaire (dialogic, condensed, evaluative critical, positive regulatory, expanded, elicited, pristine/spontaneous), the 2015 emotional-type categories (faithful friend, ambivalent parent, proud rival, helpless child), the speed of inner thought (Sean Shannon's 'To be or not to be' soliloquy, Lev Vygotsky's work on private speech and child development), people who lack inner speech (anendophasia, with conflicting prevalence estimates), Russell Hurlbert's Descriptive Experience Sampling, the efference copy and its link to schizophrenia's verbal hallucinations, purposes of inner speech, and anecdotes about falling asleep and inner speech in deaf people. The episode closes with a listener email about Tony Packo's in Toledo and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and framing inner speech
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with a playful demonstration of private speech and introduce inner speech as a better term than inner monologue. They note the topic is hard to study and reach a consensus on.

segments.title: Difficulty of studying inner voice and uses of inner speech
segments.summary: They discuss William James's comparison of studying inner speech to turning up lights to see the dark, the reliance on self-reported data, and the functions of inner speech such as motivation, memory, problem solving and self-regulation.

segments.title: Varieties of inner speech: dialogic, condensed, other people
segments.summary: The hosts describe the VISC questionnaire by Simon McCarthy-Jones and Charles Fernyhough and categories such as dialogic inner speech, condensed inner speech, and 'other people' voices, with examples like keys-phone-wallet and an Italian-couple inner argument from a Guardian article. They also discuss evaluative and positive regulatory speech and basketball visualization.

segments.title: Expanded, elicited, pristine speech and emotional types
segments.summary: They cover expanded speech used in rehearsal, elicited speech prompted by outside cues like rhyming tasks, and pristine spontaneous speech described by Russell Hurlbert. They also discuss the 2015 emotional categories by Malgorzata Pulchaska-Wasil: faithful friend, ambivalent parent, proud rival, and helpless child replacing 'calm optimist'.

segments.title: Speed of inner thought and Sean Shannon
segments.summary: The hosts discuss inner speech being faster than spoken speech. A 1990 study found participants could think over 4,000 words per minute, compared with the roughly 655 words-per-minute record held by Sean Shannon, who delivered Hamlet's soliloquy in 23.8 seconds.

segments.title: Development of inner speech and Vygotsky
segments.summary: They explain how Lev Vygotsky's 1930s work showed children move from private speech to inner speech, around age six or seven, and how his ideas, translated in the 1950s, contrasted with Jean Piaget's view. The hosts also mention Emily's habit of spelling words with her thumb when stressed.

segments.title: People without inner speech: anendophasia
segments.summary: They discuss estimates of people without inner speech, with Nedergaard and Lupyan proposing five to ten percent and Russell Hurlbert suggesting fifty to seventy percent. Fernyhough objected to the term anendophasia, and the hosts discuss sociopaths and inner dialogue.

segments.title: Verbal memory study and other modes of thought
segments.summary: A 2024 study linked low inner speech to weaker verbal memory. The hosts discuss inner seeing, unsymbolized thinking, emotion-driven and sensory-awareness thinking, and a possible link to dyslexia and visual thinking.

segments.title: Josh's imagery test and thought-without-words
segments.summary: Josh describes testing himself by summoning a watering can image without words, and the hosts reflect on visual thinking and whether inner voices can be controlled.

segments.title: Ruby and Magdalena Bay aside
segments.summary: A brief personal aside: Ruby's report that her inner voice says 'find Josh kill Josh', and a recommendation of the artist Magdalena Bay.

segments.title: Russell Hurlbert and Descriptive Experience Sampling
segments.summary: The hosts describe Russell Hurlbert's Descriptive Experience Sampling method, in which participants log thoughts when a beeper sounds and then undergo extensive interviews. They note how it reduces subjectivity, and Chuck and Josh debate whether Rosebud was a sled.

segments.title: Efference copy and brain imaging
segments.summary: Josh explains the efference copy, a brain prediction signal sent before speech that also occurs in a cruder form during inner speech. The hosts note that brain imaging shows regions for both speech and inner speech, with some differences.

segments.title: Schizophrenia, verbal hallucinations and self-talk
segments.summary: They explain that impairment in the efference copy process may explain why some people with schizophrenia experience verbal hallucinations as external voices. They also discuss links between negative self-talk and anxiety, OCD, and depression.

segments.title: Purposes of inner speech and video game overthinking
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how inner speech supports child development, executive functioning, decision-making, emotional regulation, and performance. Josh and the hosts share anecdotes about planning actions and overthinking video games.

segments.title: Inner speech across languages, deaf people, and sleep
segments.summary: They discuss whether fluency in a second language brings an inner voice in that language, how deaf people may think in sign language, and Justin Hopkins's 'island in a sea of void' description of rare thoughts. They also discuss inner speech turning nonsensical as a person drifts toward sleep.

segments.title: Viral tweet about inner voice spectrum
segments.summary: Josh describes a widely shared tweet from around 2020 in which people discovered that others do or do not have an inner voice, and the hosts note that it shows inner speech is a spectrum.

segments.title: Listener email about Tony Packo's in Toledo
segments.summary: A listener named Alex writes about Tony Packo's in Toledo, a Hungarian-founded hot dog restaurant where celebrities sign hot dog buns, and the hosts discuss its stuffed cabbage and a possible key to the city.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts mention the email address and the show credit.
